title: Human-in-the-loop is not one thing: a small probe on CollabSkill trajectories
body:
I have been thinking about an adjacent question to **CollabSkill**:

> CollabSkill asks how much skill the human and the agent contribute. Could it also be useful to label **why the human had to intervene at all**?

This came from a practical problem in a system I am building, EckoYa. We kept finding that "human in the loop" collapsed very different things:

- a human choosing what they actually want,
- a human adding domain expertise,
- a human granting legitimate authority,
- a human checking whether something is correct,
- a human manually relaying state between systems,
- and a human repairing a failed artifact/tool/access boundary.

Those are all human turns, but removing them would have very different consequences.

## A quick attempt - and where it broke

I pulled the public SALT-NLP/cogym-collabskill-trajectories dataset (CC BY 4.0) and used a deterministic extractor to identify **1,058 conversational user follow-up turns** after the initial request.

That number is only a search universe. I am **not** claiming label prevalence.

My first coding vocabulary was:

PREFERENCE | EXPERTISE | AUTHORITY | VERIFICATION | RELAY

It broke quickly.

One trajectory has a user report that the generated file cannot be opened and asks for a working link/new file. That turn is not preference, expertise, authority, verification, or simple relay. The human is doing **recovery work because the collaboration failed**.

So the current exploratory vocabulary became:

- **INTENT / PREFERENCE** - change or clarify target, scope, format, trade-off, or subjective definition of good
- **EXPERTISE** - contribute domain knowledge/correction
- **AUTHORITY** - provide legitimate permission/approval
- **VERIFICATION** - inspect correctness, provenance, readiness, or post-condition
- **RELAY** - move state/information between systems that could in principle be bridged
- **RECOVERY** - intervene because execution, access, artifact delivery, or another boundary failed

Labels can be multi-valued.

## A few examples from the public trajectories

- "cut the word length to under 1,000 words" -> INTENT/PREFERENCE
- "The permissions have been updated. Transfer this data to the sheet." -> AUTHORITY + RELAY
- "Show me the 10 rows in a readable table here before I open the file." -> VERIFICATION
- "Approved installation of Pandoc." -> AUTHORITY
- "The summary finding tab is returning all #NA... simulate a 5% increase... ensure the visualizations are working." -> RECOVERY + VERIFICATION
- "I am unable to open the file... provide a link or a possible new file..." -> RECOVERY

The interesting thing to me is that **human skill and human necessity look like different axes**.

A strong human may contribute a lot because the task genuinely needs human judgment. But a strong human may also contribute a lot because the system forced them to relay state or repair broken execution.

Those cases should probably not be optimized the same way.

## A possible decomposition

Very tentatively:

productive human load = intent + expertise + authority + necessary verification

coordination tax = avoidable relay + avoidable recovery + avoidable verification

I would **not** optimize for minimizing all human intervention.

Removing RELAY may reduce burden without reducing agency.

Removing AUTHORITY can make a system look more autonomous while actually crossing a governance boundary.

Removing INTENT can produce a very efficient system that optimizes the wrong thing.

And RECOVERY seems worth measuring explicitly: if humans repeatedly step in because files are missing, permissions fail, tools cannot reach a surface, or state is lost, that is collaboration cost that a task score may hide.

## What would falsify this?

I would abandon or heavily revise the idea if:

1. the labels cannot achieve reasonable inter-rater agreement;
2. they collapse mostly into generic preference;
3. they add no explanatory/predictive value beyond existing trajectory features;
4. relay/recovery cannot be distinguished without private state unavailable in the trace;
5. reducing apparent coordination tax harms outcome quality or human agency;
6. this is already captured by a better construct in HCI/CSCW that I have missed.

The next experiment I would run is deliberately small: **20-50 turns, two independent annotators, disagreement analysis before any benchmark or metric.**

### Question

For people working on CollabSkill / human-agent collaboration: **does an orthogonal "why was the human intervention necessary?" label add useful signal, or is this already represented by a better construct/framework?**

I would especially appreciate counterexamples that break the taxonomy.

Sources:
- CollabSkill: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09833
- Public trajectories: https://huggingface.co/datasets/SALT-NLP/cogym-collabskill-trajectories
- Collaborative Gym: https://github.com/SALT-NLP/collaborative-gym

- Kayky, building EckoYa

nodes.body: @shaoyijia - tagging you once because this probe came directly from the public CollabSkill trajectories. The part I am least confident about is whether "human necessity" is actually orthogonal to skill, or whether HCI/CSCW already has a better construct for it. A counterexample would be more useful to me than agreement.
